title: James Webb Telescope catches big surprise from a tiny world
excerpt: Chariklo is only 250 kilometers wide and lies roughly 17 times farther from the Sun than Earth.
content:
Don Davis

Updated Tue, September 15, 2026 at 3:24 PM UTC

(NewsNation) — A tiny, distant world has just delivered a big surprise: its rings are changing. Astronomers using the James Webb Space Telescope have found that Chariklo, a small icy body orbiting between Saturn and Uranus, has undergone dramatic changes in its two narrow rings in just a few years.

The discovery, published Sept. 9 in Science Advances, suggests ring systems around small bodies may be far more dynamic than scientists once believed.

Big changes for a small system

Chariklo is only about 250 kilometers (155 miles) wide and lies roughly 17 times farther from the Sun than Earth. Its two rings were discovered in 2013, surprising astronomers as such structures had been associated primarily with giant planets.

Phys.org, which reported on the study, noted that even Webb cannot photograph Chariklo's rings directly. Instead, researchers watched a distant star's light briefly fade as Chariklo and its rings passed in front of it — a technique known as a stellar occultation.

The results from an Oct. 18, 2022, Webb observation were striking. Compared with previous occultations, the inner ring, known as C1R, appeared substantially more opaque, while the outer ring, C2R, appeared significantly less opaque. Study leader Pablo Santos-Sanz of the Institute of Astrophysics of Andalusia said “opposite changes” in the two rings point to a system that is actively evolving. Phys.org highlighted the finding as evidence that Chariklo's rings can change on timescales of only a few years.

The observation itself was a technological feat. The team had to precisely calculate Chariklo's orbit, the position of the background star using data from the European Space Agency's Gaia mission, and Webb's own trajectory around the Sun-Earth L2 point.

During the occultation, Chariklo was moving relative to Webb at only about 2.5 kilometers per second, allowing the telescope to obtain exceptionally detailed information about rings that are otherwise invisible. Space.com described the observation as an important milestone for Webb, while SpaceDaily likewise reported the discovery as evidence that Chariklo's two-ring system is changing over time.

What is driving the transformation remains a mystery

The researchers caution the difference could reflect genuine evolution of the rings, effects associated with observations at different wavelengths, or a combination of factors. But the discovery is already forcing astronomers to reconsider how these delicate structures form, evolve and remain stable. As Santos-Sanz put it, detecting such changes opens a new window onto the evolution of Chariklo — and potentially other ring systems across the Solar System.
